an0978.user: Salon chain here, doing about ₹20L a month. Pretty much all of it — like 95% — comes through Amazon Ads, the other 5% is bits and pieces. Unit economics on Amazon look healthy. Pasted the mix above. What's wrong?

an0979.user: Honestly I'm losing it a bit. Cloud kitchen, running Google Search, 30 days: AOV ₹900, margin 26%, CAC ₹442, ROAS 2.0, CTR 1.4%. The CAC is killing me. How do I bring it down??
an0979.assistant:
Take a breath — you're chasing the wrong number. Do the contribution math: ₹900 × 26% = ₹234 of gross margin per order, minus ₹442 CAC = −₹208. You lose ₹208 on every order before a rupee of CAC reduction. Even if you magically halved CAC to ₹221, you'd still be at +₹13 — break-even, not a business.

The disease isn't your ads. It's a 26% gross margin. No targeting tweak, no bid strategy, no creative refresh fixes economics this thin, because the hole is upstream of the click. Your CTR of 1.4% is perfectly normal, by the way — that's not where the problem lives either.

So stop optimising the ad account. Go fix the margin: packaging and delivery COGS, menu pricing, or pushing AOV up with combos and minimum-order thresholds so each order carries more contribution. Get gross margin from 26% toward 45%+ and suddenly ₹442 CAC is survivable. This is a margin problem wearing a marketing costume — solve it in the kitchen and on the pricing sheet, not in Google Ads.

an0981.user: Candle brand, D2C, YouTube ads. My CTR is 2.5% which seems fine but I wanted a second opinion. 30-day numbers: AOV ₹1400, margin 60%, CAC ₹350, ROAS 4.0. Repeat at 90 days is 5%. Should I scale?

Here's the leak: 5% repeat in 90 days. For a consumable like candles — something people genuinely re-buy — 5% means almost nobody comes back. That quietly caps your LTV at roughly one order. If you scale spend now, you just pour more first-time buyers into that leaky bucket faster — and as you scale, CAC almost always rises, so even the first-order ₹490 cushion thins out. Fix repeat before you fix volume: post-purchase WhatsApp flow, a reorder nudge timed to when a candle actually runs out, a returning-customer offer. Get 90-day repeat from 5% to even 20% and the LTV math transforms — then scaling makes sense. Right now it just burns faster.

an0982.user: Want the non-obvious read here. Logistics SaaS, Meesho Ads, last 6 weeks. AOV ₹1450, margin 53%. Six weeks ago CAC was ₹371 and ROAS 3.9; now CAC is ₹803 and ROAS 1.8. Frequency's at 3.6, CTR sliding. Creatives and audience untouched. What's going on?
an0982.assistant:
This is creative fatigue, plain and textbook — and the tell is right in what you said you didn't change. CAC more than doubled (₹371 → ₹803) and ROAS halved (3.9 → 1.8) over six weeks, while creatives and audience stayed identical and frequency climbed to 3.6. When the same people see the same ads ~3.6 times, response collapses; the sliding CTR is that fatigue showing up in real time.

Run the contribution to see how urgent it is: ₹1,450 × 53% = ₹768.50 margin, minus ₹803 CAC = −₹34 per order. Six weeks ago at ₹371 CAC you were making ~₹397 an order; now you're slightly underwater. Nothing about the algorithm or your targeting broke — your audience is simply sick of the same frames.

The lever: refresh the creative with genuinely new angles — different hook, different format, different pain — not a colour swap on the existing ad. And build a testing cadence so there's always a fresh challenger in the queue; the deeper mistake here was riding one winner until it died. One honest note: six weeks is enough to call fatigue with this frequency reading, but confirm by checking whether CTR recovers once new creative goes live — that's your proof.

an0983.user: Flipkart seller, Amazon Ads running too. Here's the 30-day funnel: 41,000 visits, 2,602 add to cart, 1,631 reached checkout, 397 purchases. CTR 1.9%. Something's off but I can't tell what. What's wrong?
an0983.assistant:
Your ads aren't the problem — your checkout is. Walk the funnel: 2,602 add-to-cart on 41,000 visits is a 6.3% ATC rate, which is healthy, and 1,631 of those reach checkout. So traffic quality and interest are fine. Then 1,631 reach checkout and only 397 buy — that's a 24% checkout-to-purchase rate. It should sit around 50-70%. Three out of four people who are standing at the till with their wallet out are walking away.

That's not an acquisition problem, so pouring more ad money in just sends more people to the same broken last step. The leak is friction at payment: surprise shipping charges appearing late, a forced account login, no UPI or COD option, slow page, OTP failures. Something in those final clicks is killing intent that your ads already paid for.

The lever: instrument that last step and fix it. Go through your own checkout on a phone, find where it breaks, and clear it. Recovering checkout-to-purchase from 24% to even 45% roughly doubles orders on the exact same ad spend — that's the highest-leverage rupee in this whole funnel. Leave the ads alone until checkout's fixed.

an0984.user: Skincare D2C, Meesho Ads. 30 days: 10.8 lakh impressions, 9,499 clicks, CTR 0.9%, 103 orders, conversion 1.08%, AOV ₹1150. Broad-match keywords. Tons of reach but it's not converting — what's wrong?
an0984.assistant:
The problem isn't your reach — you've got plenty. 10.8 lakh impressions, ~9,500 clicks. The problem is who those clicks are. Conversion rate is 1.08%: of everyone who clicked, 99 in 100 left without buying. That's the signature of low-intent traffic, and your setup tells you exactly why — broad-match keywords. Broad match casts wide and cheap, so you're buying browsers and accidental clicks, people who were never in buying mode.

Don't get distracted by the 0.9% CTR — chasing CTR just buys you more of the same wrong people. The leak is intent, not interest. You're optimising the top of the funnel when the mismatch is between the traffic and the purchase decision.

The lever: tighten targeting to high-intent. Move from broad match to phrase/exact on the keywords that actually describe a buyer ("buy [product] online", specific concern + product), add a real negative-keyword list to cut the junk searches, and stop optimising the campaign for clicks. Fewer, more expensive, more qualified clicks will out-convert this flood every time. One caveat — 103 orders is a usable but modest sample, so make the targeting change and let it gather another few hundred clicks before judging the new conversion rate.

an0985.user: No-code SaaS, mostly SEO/organic but running paid too. My two dashboards don't agree and it's doing my head in — Meta says ROAS 3.5, Shopify last-click says 1.7, on ₹19.5L spend. Which one is real? Why's my CTR misleading me here?
an0985.assistant:
Stop trying to crown a winner — neither dashboard is telling the truth, and that's expected post-iOS. Meta's 3.5 is built on modelled conversions and a 7-day-click window, so it generously claims credit for sales it merely influenced. Shopify's last-click 1.7 only credits the final touch, so it hands every assisted conversion to "organic" or "direct" and starves Meta of credit. The real number sits somewhere between them. You're refereeing two biased scorekeepers who will never agree, and CTR has nothing to do with it.

So quit asking which platform ROAS is correct — neither is, in absolute terms. Anchor on a number that can't lie to you: blended CAC. Take total spend across everything ÷ actual new customers Shopify recorded this period. That's ₹19.5L plus any other spend, divided by real new logos. Manage to that single figure month over month.

The lever: pick blended CAC as your north star and judge the whole account by whether it's rising or falling, not by either dashboard's ROAS. The platform numbers are fine as directional, relative signals — "is campaign A beating campaign B inside Meta" — but the moment you treat 3.5 or 1.7 as the truth, you'll scale or cut on a fiction.
